Learning Objectives
Discuss normal growth and development of the hip joint.
Explain the epidemiology, pathoanatomy, risk factors, and natural history of developmental
dysplasia of the hip.
Perform an appropriate work up of patients in whom developmental dysplasia of the hip is
suspected.
Review the nonsurgical and surgical management of developmental dysplasia of the hip and
the risks associated with various treatment options.

Definition
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) refers to the spectrum of pathologic conditions
involving the developing femoral head and acetabulum.
Dysplasia: radiographic or ultrasonographic finding of a shallow acetabulum
Subluxation: femoral head is not in full contact with the acetabulum
Dislocation: femoral head is not in contact with the acetabulum
Teratologic dislocation of the hip occurs in utero and is irreducible on neonatal examination.
A pseudoacetabulum usually is present. This condition always accompanies other congenital
anomalies or neuromuscular conditions, most often arthrogryposis and myelomeningocele.
Epidemiology/Etiology
DDH is the most common abnormality in newborn infants.
Clinical hip instability ranges from 1% to 3% in neonates
Ultrasonographic hip dysplasia ranges from 5% to 15% in neonates
More than 90% of hip dysplasia presents in adolescents or adults.
80% of affected children are female.
The left hip is more commonly involved (60%), with bilateral involvement occurring in 20% of
patients.
The condition is more common in Native Americans and people of Scandinavian descent; DDH
is rarely observed in African Americans.
The etiology of DDH is multifactorial (genetic, hormonal, mechanical, and environmental).
Anatomy/Pathoanatomy
Normal growth and development
Hip begins development from primitive mesenchymal cells during the sixth intrauterine week
and is fully formed by the eleventh intrauterine week.
Most acetabular development is determined by approximately age 8 years.
Pathoanatomy
Most abnormality is on the acetabular side.
The femoral-sided changes typically result from increased femoral anteversion, coxa valga,
and pressure variance from subluxation or dislocation (Figure 1).

Natural History
40% of osteoarthritis previously thought to be idiopathic is the result of unmanaged
acetabular dysplasia.1
The same is true for two-thirds of women with osteoarthritis.1

Stable (negative Ortolani and Barlow tests)

junction of the H-line and P-line. The H-point is the midpoint of the superior margin of the
ossified metaphysis. Grade I, the H-point is at or medial to the P-line. Grade II, the H-point is
lateral to the P-line and at or medial to the D-line. Grade III, the H-point is lateral to the D-line
and at or inferior to the H-line. Grade IV, the H-point is superior to the H-line. (Reproduced
with permission from Narayanan U, Mulpuri K, Sankar WN, Clarke NM, Hosalkar H, Price CT:
International Hip Dysplasia Institute: Reliability of a new radiographic classification for
developmental dysplasia of the hip. J Pediatr Orthop 2015;35[5]:478-484.)
Associated Pathology
Metatarsus adductus
Torticollis
Calcaneovalgus foot deformity
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Risk factors
Female sex, firstborn child, breech presentation, family history of DDH
Disorders of intrauterine positioning/packing/molding, such as congenital dislocation of the
knee, congenital muscular torticollis, and metatarsus adductus
12% to 33% of affected children have a family history of DDH.
Risk is 6% with one affected sibling, 12% with one affected parent, and 36% with a parent
and sibling affected.
Physical Examination
Routine neonatal examination is essential for early detection.
Clinical presentation varies with age. Before approximately 6 months, the key clinical finding
is instability of the hip, whereas children older than approximately 6 months
characteristically have asymmetry in abduction profile and apparent limb shortening (in
unilateral dislocations).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000575
5/22

Hip clicks and asymmetric skin folds are unreliable, nonspecific physical examination
findings.
In toddlers, restricted motion may be accompanied by a limb-length discrepancy, a limp, or a
waddling gait. Toddlers with bilateral hip dislocations often present with hyperlordosis of the
lumbar spine.
Adolescents may manifest all the aforementioned signs and symptoms in addition to fatigue
and discomfort in the hip, thigh, or knee.
Accuracy of infant examination is enhanced with a relaxed, warm, and well-fed patient.
The Galeazzi test is performed with the patient in the supine position and the hips and knees
flexed to 90°. The test is positive if the knee on the involved side is lower than the
contralateral knee. The test is positive only in unilateral subluxation or dislocation of the hip.
The Barlow test is used to determine if the hip is dislocatable and is performed by applying a
gentle posterolateral force to the leg with the hip in a flexed and adducted position (Figure
3).
Figure 3 Illustration shows the Barlow test. The test is positive if the hip on the affected side
subluxates or dislocates. (Reproduced from Spiegel DA, Sarwark JF: Developmental dysplasia

of the hip, in Sarwark JF, ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2010, p 1050-1055.)
The Ortolani test is used to assess reducibility of the hip in question and is performed by
abducting and lifting the proximal femur anteriorly (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration shows the Ortolani test. The test is positive if the dislocated head is
reducible. A palpable clunk often is felt as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum.
(Reproduced from Spiegel DA, Sarwark JF: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, in Sarwark JF,
ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2010, p 1050-1055.)
Range of motion testing of the hip is important; a decrease in abduction is the most sensitive
test result for DDH after approximately age 6 months. Range of motion may be normal in
children younger than 6 months because adduction contractures typically have not yet
developed.
Imaging Studies
Ultrasonography

Universal newborn screening remains controversial; however, it is a standard of care in many
European countries, such as Germany and Switzerland.2
Ultrasonography should be performed for infants with risk factors for DDH (eg, breech, family
history), including suspicious examination, parental concern, or history of tight lower extremity
swaddling.1 The screening should be delayed until 46 weeks gestational age because
ligamentous laxity may provide a false sense of hip instability in the early newborn period.3
In the first 4 to 6 months of life, ultrasonography can help confirm a diagnosis of stable DDH.
Radiographic evaluation of a patient with an unossified femoral epiphysis may pose a
diagnostic challenge. Ultrasonography also can be performed document dynamic reducibility
and stability of the hip in an infant being treated via a Pavlik harness or brace.
Reference parameters (Figure 5)
After 46 weeks adjusted gestational age, the alpha angle should be greater than 60° with a
normal beta angle of less than 55°. (The alpha angle is formed by a reference line along the
iliac bone and a line along the osseous roof of the acetabulum; the beta angle is formed by a
line through the central portion of the cartilaginous anlage and the iliac reference line and
represents the cartilaginous roof of the acetabulum.)
The acetabulum should cover more than 50% of the femoral head.

The Perkin line is drawn perpendicular to the Hilgenreiner line at the lateral edge of the
acetabulum.
The Shenton line is a continuous arch drawn along the medial border of the femoral neck
and the superior border of the obturator foramen (Figure 6). The acetabular index is the
angle formed by an oblique line through the outer edge of the acetabulum and the triradiate
cartilage and the Hilgenreiner line along the sourcil. The acetabular index should be less than
30° at age 6 months, 25° at age 12 months, and less than 23° at age 24 months4 (Figure 7).
Figure 6 AP view illustration of the pelvis shows reference lines and angles used in the
radiographic evaluation of developmental dysplasia of the hip. (Reproduced from Matheney
TH, Upasani VV: The pediatric hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1394-
1412.)

Figure 7 AP radiograph of the pelvis of a 6-month-old child demonstrates dysplastic
acetabular indices. (Courtesy of Courtney Selberg, MD, Denver, CO.)
The lateral center-edge angle of Wiberg is the angle formed by a vertical line through the
center of the femoral head (assuming a level pelvis) and an oblique line through the lateral
edge of the sourcil from the center of the femoral head. An angle greater than 25° is normal,
and an angle of less than 22° is considered abnormal in a skeletally mature pelvis5 (Figure 8).
The lateral center-edge angle of Wiberg may be challenging to properly draw in a patient with
an incompletely ossified femoral head and acetabular rim but can be applied to pelves as
young as age 6 years6 (Table 2).

Figure 8 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates the lateral center-edge angle of Wiberg, which is
formed from two lines passing from the center of the femoral head. One line extends to the
lateral edge of the sclerotic margin of the acetabulum (sourcil), and the other line is

observed) or the base of the ischium. (Courtesy of Courtney Selberg, MD, Denver, CO.)
Computed Tomography
CT is a useful three-dimensional imaging modality to confirm adequate reduction of the
femoral head within the acetabulum, with the notable disadvantage of radiation exposure.
CT is especially useful when implants have been used or in the setting of planned surgical
treatment in walking-age children to delineate acetabular deficiency and femoral version.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is a useful imaging modality for evaluating the hips without radiation exposure and
without sedation in infants and toddlers after spica cast placement. Limited series study can
be performed to obviate the need for sedation and can accurately assess reduction of the
femoral head.7
Perfusion MRI also can be performed to assess femoral head perfusion in the spica cast after
closed reduction; however, additional study is needed to assess the efficacy of this modality.8

Arthrography
Arthrography of the hip is performed to dynamically assess the quality of a closed reduction,
with ideal reduction to the ischial limb of the acetabulum.
A medial dye pool of less than 16% of femoral head width may be a useful intraoperative
criterion for determining the adequacy of closed reduction/repositioning.9
Pathology
Impediments to reduction
Transverse acetabular ligament
Ligamentum teres
Fibrofatty tissue/pulvinar
Labrum
Anteromedial capsule
Iliopsoas and adductor tightness
Prevention
Healthy hip swaddling
A sleep sack with the infant’s legs able to freely move is preferable over including the legs in
a tight swaddle.
Do not force or maintain neonatal hip extension/adduction. This is most commonly done with
lower extremity swaddling.
Management
Management of DDH is based on age, stability, and severity of dysplasia. Obtaining and
maintaining concentric reduction and avoiding osteonecrosis likely are the main factors in
accomplishing the best long-term hip function and radiographic results (Table 3).

Residual dysplasia after hip reduction
Pelvic osteotomy may be indicated for a broken Shenton line or persistent acetabular
dysplasia. Clinical practice varies considerably with regard to pelvic osteotomy in children
older than 2 years.
The three general types of pelvic osteotomy are redirectional, reshaping, and salvage.
Redirectional: single innominate (Salter) osteotomy, triple innominate osteotomy, Bernese
periacetabular osteotomy
Reshaping: Pemberton osteotomy, Dega osteotomy, San Diego osteotomy
Salvage: Chiari osteotomy, shelf osteotomy
Nonsurgical Management
Newborns and infants younger than 6 months
A Pavlik harness is the preferred treatment option for dysplasia, subluxation, or complete
dislocation of the hip.

Proper positioning of the Pavlik harness is critical.
The hips should be flexed to 90° to 100° with mild abduction.
Excessive flexion should be avoided to decrease the risk of femoral nerve palsy (absence of
quadriceps function: hip flexion/knee extension), which should necessitate immediate
cessation of the harness.
Excessive abduction should be avoided to decrease the risk of osteonecrosis.
The duration of management varies. Most studies recommend uninterrupted management
for 6 to 12 weeks after clinical stability is achieved or until acetabular development has
normalized.10,11
Frequent (every 1 to 2 weeks) clinical and ultrasonographic examinations are necessary to
evaluate reduction and stability of the hip or hips.
Pavlik harness management should be discontinued if the dislocated hip does not reduce
within 2 to 3 weeks to avoid Pavlik harness disease (deformation of the posterosuperior
acetabular rim). Success rates higher than 90% have been reported with use of a Pavlik
harness in patients with a dislocated, reducible hip.12
Follow-up until skeletal maturity is necessary to manage recurrent instability or residual
acetabular dysplasia.13
If a Pavlik harness is unable to result in hip stability, a semirigid hip abduction orthosis may
be used.12
Surgical Management
Children aged 6 to 18 months
A Pavlik harness can be attempted; however, closed or open reduction with arthrography
under general anesthesia may be required.
Hip arthrography is used intraoperatively to confirm the adequacy of closed reduction. A
medial dye pool of less than 16% of femoral head width should be observed between the
femoral head and the ischial limb of the acetabulum9 (Figure 9).

Figure 9 Images of the pelvis of a 8-month-old child. A, AP radiograph demonstrates bilateral
International Hip Dysplasia Institute grade IV hip dislocations. AP arthrograms show
dislocation (B) and subsequent reduction (C) viewed fluoroscopically. D, Coronal MRI shows
femoral head reduction to the ischial limb of triradiate cartilage. E, Axial MRI shows
concentrically reduced hips. (Courtesy of Joseph D. Stone, MD (Chapel Hill, NC)
The safe and stable zones for abduction/adduction, flexion/extension, and internal/external
rotation should be established.
Adductor tenotomy may be used to increase this safe zone.
A spica cast is applied with the hip in the human position (hip flexion of 90° to 100° and
abduction 20° to 30° from maximal). Hip abduction should be less than 60° to minimize the
risk of osteonecrosis but greater than 40° to diminish the risk of redislocation.14
Open reduction is indicated if concentric closed reduction cannot be achieved or if excessive
abduction (>60°) is required to maintain reduction.
The goal of open reduction is to remove the obstacles to reduction and/or safely increase
stability of the hip. Impediments to congruent reduction are the iliopsoas muscle, hip
adductors, joint capsule, ligamentum teres, pulvinar, and transverse acetabular ligament. An
infolded labrum may be an impediment in some patients.
A medial or anterior approach may be used to achieve open reduction with similar rates of
osteonecrosis (almost 20%) reported in a recent meta-analysis.15
Reduction of the hip in the cast typically is confirmed via three-dimensional imaging.
Cast immobilization is performed with the use of two 6-week spica casts, with interim cast
changes and assessment of stability. An abduction brace may then be used until the
acetabulum normalizes.

Children older than 18 months
Anterior open reduction is the preferred treatment option.
Surgical treatment generally is indicated for children as old as 8 to 10 years with a unilateral
dislocation; however, this is highly controversial. After 10 years of age, the risks associated
with surgical management outweigh the advantages, and very little remodeling potential
remains. The upper age limit for surgical management of DDH in children with bilateral
dislocations typically is age 6 to 8 years.
Femoral shortening osteotomy is indicated in children with a high-riding dislocation to
achieve and maintain reduction and minimize the risk of osteonecrosis. This is necessary in
most, but not all, children older than 36 months or those with a femoral head displaced
cranially more than 30% of pelvic width.16
A pelvic osteotomy may be necessary for the management of severe acetabular dysplasia
(typical in children older than 18 to 24 months). Pelvic osteotomy notably reduces the rate of
revision surgery if performed at the time of initial surgical treatment in children in this age
group.
Principles of pelvic osteotomies for DDH
Change the pathologic mechanical environment by:
Increasing femoral head coverage via augmentation of the acetabular roof
Changing the spatial orientation of the acetabulum
Reconstructive pelvic osteotomies redirect or reshape the roof of the native acetabulum into
a more appropriate weight-bearing position. A prerequisite for reconstructive pelvic
osteotomy is a hip that can be reduced concentrically and congruently. The hip also must
have near-normal range of motion.
Redirectional pelvic osteotomies (Figure 10) include the single innominate (Salter), triple
innominate osteotomy, and periacetabular or rotational osteotomies.

Figure 10 Illustrations show redirectional pelvic osteotomy options. A, Single innominate
(Salter). B, Triple innominate. C, Bernese periacetabular. (Reproduced from Matheney TH,
Upasani VV: The pediatric hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review,

The Ganz periacetabular osteotomy or rotational acetabular osteotomies can be performed
in skeletally mature patients with a closing triradiate cartilage and residual acetabular
dysplasia without advancing arthritis (ideally Tönnis grade coxarthrosis 0 or 1).17
Reshaping pelvic osteotomies (acetabuloplasties) include the Pemberton, Dega, and San
Diego osteotomies.
Salvage osteotomies increase weight-bearing coverage by using the joint capsule interposed
between the femoral head and the bone above it. Salvage osteotomies rely on
fibrocartilaginous metaplasia of the interposed joint capsule to provide an increased
articulating surface. The intent of these osteotomies is to reduce point loading at the edge of
the acetabulum.
Salvage osteotomies typically are indicated in adolescents with severe dysplasia in whom
acetabular deficiency precludes a reconstructive osteotomy.
Salvage osteotomies include the Chiari and shelf osteotomies.
Outcomes
As many as 50% of patients who undergo successful closed reduction require secondary
surgery.18
Bernese periacetabular osteotomy is associated with a long-term survivorship (mean, 18 years)
of 74% (no conversion to total hip arthroplasty and 53% of patients are asymptomatic).19
